items.prompt: A zero-indexed array has length n. Which indices are valid when n > 0?

feedback.reason: A zero-indexed sequence of length n occupies positions 0 through n - 1.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “0 through n - 1, inclusive.” A zero-indexed array starts at position 0, so n elements occupy exactly n consecutive positions ending at n - 1. For example, length 4 gives indices 0, 1, 2, and 3; index 4 is immediately outside the array.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: A zero-indexed sequence of length n occupies positions 0 through n - 1.

items: 1 through n, inclusive. — This skips index 0 and includes the invalid index n.
0 through n, inclusive. — Index n is outside a sequence containing exactly n elements.
1 through n - 1, inclusive. — This excludes the valid first element at index 0.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_to_n: This skips index 0 and includes the invalid index n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_to_n: Index n is outside a sequence containing exactly n elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_to_n_minus_one: This excludes the valid first element at index 0.

items.prompt: A forward loop over a zero-indexed array of length n starts with i = 0, increments i by 1, and compares array[i] with array[i + 1]. Which loop condition keeps both accesses valid?

feedback.reason: Because the loop reads i + 1, the largest legal i is n - 2.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “i < n - 1”. The condition i < n - 1 produces i values from 0 through n - 2. On the final iteration, i + 1 equals n - 1, the last valid index.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Because the loop reads i + 1, the largest legal i is n - 2.

items: i < n — When i equals n - 1, the access at i + 1 becomes index n.
i <= n - 1 — This also allows i = n - 1 and therefore reads index n.
i <= n — At i = n - 1 the neighbor access already reads index n, and allowing i = n goes even farther out of bounds.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.i_less_n: When i equals n - 1, the access at i + 1 becomes index n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.i_less_equal_n_minus_one: This also allows i = n - 1 and therefore reads index n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.i_less_equal_n: At i = n - 1 the neighbor access already reads index n, and allowing i = n goes even farther out of bounds.

items.prompt: A forward scan must compare every adjacent pair in a zero-indexed array of length n >= 2 using array[i - 1] and array[i]. At which index should i begin?

feedback.reason: Starting at 1 makes i - 1 equal 0 on the first iteration.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “1”. Index 0 has no previous element. Starting at 1 covers the first adjacent pair, array[0] and array[1], without reading a negative index.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Starting at 1 makes i - 1 equal 0 on the first iteration.

items: 0 — The first access to i - 1 would use index -1.
2 — This is safe but skips the first adjacent pair.
n - 1 — This inspects only the final pair instead of scanning all adjacent pairs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_zero: The first access to i - 1 would use index -1.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_two: This is safe but skips the first adjacent pair.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_n_minus_one: This inspects only the final pair instead of scanning all adjacent pairs.

items.prompt: A positive-length contiguous window starts at a known nonnegative index start in a zero-indexed array of length n and contains w elements. Which condition states that the whole window is inside the array?

feedback.reason: A window [start, start + w) is valid when its exclusive end does not exceed n.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “start + w <= n”. The last included index is start + w - 1. Requiring start + w <= n is equivalent to requiring that last index to be at most n - 1.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: A window [start, start + w) is valid when its exclusive end does not exceed n.

items: start + w < n — This incorrectly rejects the valid window whose exclusive end is exactly n.
start + w <= n - 1 — This is one position too strict because start + w is an exclusive boundary.
start <= n — A legal start alone does not guarantee that the remaining w elements fit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_plus_w_lt_n: This incorrectly rejects the valid window whose exclusive end is exactly n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_plus_w_le_n_minus_one: This is one position too strict because start + w is an exclusive boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_le_n: A legal start alone does not guarantee that the remaining w elements fit.

items.prompt: A linear scan uses `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` and reads only array[i]. What happens when n = 0?

options.text: The loop executes once and reads array[0].
The loop executes zero times, so no array access occurs.
The loop must execute once to confirm the array is empty.

feedback.reason: The initial condition 0 < 0 is false, so the body is skipped.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “The loop executes zero times, so no array access occurs.” The condition is checked before the body: with i = 0 and n = 0, 0 < 0 is false. A half-open scan from 0 to n therefore handles empty input without a special iteration, provided every access is inside the guarded body.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The initial condition 0 < 0 is false, so the body is skipped.

items: The loop executes once and reads array[0]. — The loop condition is checked before the first body execution.
The loop reads array[-1]. — The loop never computes or reads a negative index.
The loop must execute once to confirm the array is empty. — Emptiness is already represented by the failed loop condition.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reads_index_zero: The loop condition is checked before the first body execution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reads_negative_one: The loop never computes or reads a negative index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.requires_special_iteration: Emptiness is already represented by the failed loop condition.

items.prompt: How many adjacent pairs exist in an array of length n?

feedback.reason: Each adjacent pair connects one index to the next, producing n - 1 pairs when n is positive.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “max(0, n - 1)”. Lengths 0 and 1 contain no adjacent pair. For n >= 2, the pairs begin at indices 0 through n - 2, giving n - 1 pairs.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Each adjacent pair connects one index to the next, producing n - 1 pairs when n is positive.

items: n — The final element has no next element, so there are fewer pairs than elements.
n + 1 — A pair count cannot exceed the number of boundaries between consecutive elements.
Exactly one — Arrays of length 0 or 1 have none, while longer arrays can have many.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n: The final element has no next element, so there are fewer pairs than elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_plus_one: A pair count cannot exceed the number of boundaries between consecutive elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_one: Arrays of length 0 or 1 have none, while longer arrays can have many.

items.prompt: A reverse scan must visit every index of a non-empty, zero-indexed array of length n exactly once. Which index sequence is correct?

feedback.reason: The last valid index is n - 1, and index 0 must still be included.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “n - 1, n - 2, ..., 0”. Starting at n would be out of bounds. Stopping at 1 would omit the first element.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The last valid index is n - 1, and index 0 must still be included.

items: n, n - 1, ..., 0 — Length n makes n - 1 the last valid index, so beginning at n is immediately out of bounds.
n - 1, n - 2, ..., 1 — This skips the valid element at index 0.
0, 1, ..., n - 1 — This visits the same indices but in forward rather than reverse order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_to_zero: Length n makes n - 1 the last valid index, so beginning at n is immediately out of bounds.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_minus_one_to_one: This skips the valid element at index 0.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_to_n_minus_one: This visits the same indices but in forward rather than reverse order.

items.prompt: A valid half-open range [start, end), where start <= end, is used to describe a slice. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The last included index is end.
The range length is end - start.
The range is empty when start equals end.

feedback.reason: Half-open ranges include the lower bound and exclude the upper bound.

blocks.text: The correct statements are “Index end is excluded.”, “The range length is end - start.”, and “The range is empty when start equals end.” Starting at start and stopping before end visits end - start integer positions. For [2, 5), those positions are 2, 3, and 4; when both boundaries are 2, no position is visited.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Half-open ranges include the lower bound and exclude the upper bound.

items: The last included index is end. — The upper boundary is excluded, so end cannot be the last included index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_index_end: The upper boundary is excluded, so end cannot be the last included index.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.end_excluded: Excluding the upper bound is the defining property of a half-open range.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.length_end_minus_start: The number of integer indices from start up to but not including end is end - start.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.empty_when_equal: No integer index lies between equal lower and upper boundaries.

items.prompt: A scan reads array[i - 1], array[i], and array[i + 1] in a zero-indexed array of length n >= 3. Which values of i are legal?

feedback.reason: The left neighbor requires i >= 1, and the right neighbor requires i <= n - 2.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “1 through n - 2, inclusive.” The left access requires i - 1 >= 0, so i >= 1. The right access requires i + 1 <= n - 1, so i <= n - 2. Intersecting the two constraints gives 1 <= i <= n - 2; without the stated n >= 3 precondition, that interval would be empty for shorter arrays.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The left neighbor requires i >= 1, and the right neighbor requires i <= n - 2.

items: 0 through n - 1, inclusive. — At i = 0 the left access uses -1, while at i = n - 1 the right access uses n.
1 through n - 1, inclusive. — At i = n - 1, the right-neighbor access uses index n.
0 through n - 2, inclusive. — At i = 0, the left-neighbor access uses index -1.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_through_n_minus_one: At i = 0 the left access uses -1, while at i = n - 1 the right access uses n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_through_n_minus_one: At i = n - 1, the right-neighbor access uses index n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_through_n_minus_two: At i = 0, the left-neighbor access uses index -1.

items.prompt: Which tests are especially important for finding index-boundary defects? Select all that apply.

options.text: An input exactly as long as the required neighborhood or window.

feedback.reason: Boundary defects concentrate around the smallest legal and illegal input sizes.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Empty input.”, “A one-element input.”, “An input exactly as long as the required neighborhood or window.”. Empty and singleton inputs test whether the loop should execute at all. An input exactly matching the required access width verifies the first and last legal iteration.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Boundary defects concentrate around the smallest legal and illegal input sizes.

items: Only one large random input. — A large random case may never isolate the exact first, last, or no-iteration boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_large_random: A large random case may never isolate the exact first, last, or no-iteration boundary.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.empty_input: It reveals unconditional first-element reads and loops that should execute zero times.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.single_element: It distinguishes element scans from pair or neighborhood scans.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.minimum_valid_window: It checks whether the implementation accepts exactly one legal placement without running past the end.

items.prompt: At each loop boundary of a stable in-place compaction, read is the number of input elements already processed and write is the number of retained elements already written. Which invariant ensures that the output boundary never overtakes the input boundary?

options.text: read begins at -1 and remains negative until a value is retained

feedback.reason: The write boundary cannot move beyond the number of positions already read.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “0 <= write <= read <= n”. The processed prefix is array[0..read), and its retained values occupy array[0..write). Because every retained value must come from an element already processed, write cannot exceed read. For example, after processing five elements and retaining three, read = 5 and write = 3; the next retained value is written at index 3, still within the processed prefix.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The write boundary cannot move beyond the number of positions already read.

items: 0 <= read <= write <= n — This would permit writing positions that have not yet been justified by processed input.
write is always n — The write index should reflect retained output length, which can be smaller than n.
read begins at -1 and remains negative until a value is retained — A forward compaction scan can begin at index 0 without using a negative read position.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_le_write: This would permit writing positions that have not yet been justified by processed input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.write_equals_n: The write index should reflect retained output length, which can be smaller than n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_negative: A forward compaction scan can begin at index 0 without using a negative read position.

items.prompt: A sorted array is collapsed in place so each distinct value appears once. Why does merely comparing adjacent values not complete the task?

options.text: Adjacent values in a sorted array can never be equal.
The algorithm must also track where the next retained value is written and return the logical result length.
No additional logic is needed because reading duplicates removes them automatically.
The only missing step is restoring every value to its original index.

feedback.reason: Detection and output-boundary maintenance are separate responsibilities.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “The algorithm must also track where the next retained value is written and return the logical result length.” Adjacent comparison only decides whether the current value is new; it does not move that value or define the output boundary. For [1, 1, 2], the second 1 is skipped, 2 is written at index 1, and the returned logical length is 2, so only the prefix [1, 2] is part of the result.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Detection and output-boundary maintenance are separate responsibilities.

items: Adjacent values in a sorted array can never be equal. — Sorting groups equal values, so adjacent equality is exactly what the scan uses.
No additional logic is needed because reading duplicates removes them automatically. — Reading or detecting a duplicate does not mutate the output by itself.
The only missing step is restoring every value to its original index. — Sorting generally changes original positions, and this contract concerns a sorted in-place result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_values_never_equal: Sorting groups equal values, so adjacent equality is exactly what the scan uses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates_removed_automatically: Reading or detecting a duplicate does not mutate the output by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_preserves_original_indices: Sorting generally changes original positions, and this contract concerns a sorted in-place result.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for deriving a safe loop boundary from the indices used inside the loop.

elements.text: List every indexed access made from the loop variable.
Require each accessed index to stay within 0 through n - 1.
Intersect the lower and upper constraints on the loop variable.
Check the first and last permitted iterations explicitly.

feedback.reason: Safe bounds are derived from actual accesses rather than memorized loop templates.

blocks.text: Suppose the body reads array[i - 1], array[i], and array[i + 2]. Listing the accesses exposes the constraints i - 1 >= 0 and i + 2 <= n - 1. Their intersection is 1 <= i <= n - 3. Substituting i = 1 and i = n - 3 verifies that the first and last permitted iterations touch indices 0 and n - 1 without crossing either boundary.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Safe bounds are derived from actual accesses rather than memorized loop templates.

items: List accesses first; otherwise an offset such as i + 2 can be missed.
Translate each access into a bound before trying to choose a loop template.
Intersect the bounds because every access must be valid on the same iteration.
Test both endpoints of the derived interval; testing only a middle value cannot expose an off-by-one boundary.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for locating and correcting a suspected off-by-one error in an indexed scan.

elements.text: List every indexed expression evaluated by one loop iteration.
Derive the legal interval for the loop variable from those expressions.
Compare the derived interval with the loop's initialization and stopping condition.
Trace the corrected loop on the smallest legal input and the next-smaller input.

feedback.reason: The safe interval must come from every indexed expression before the implemented loop bounds can be checked or corrected.

blocks.text: For accesses array[i] and array[i + 1], the index expressions imply 0 <= i and i + 1 <= n - 1, hence 0 <= i <= n - 2. A loop ending at i = n - 1 can then be identified as one iteration too long and corrected to i < n - 1. With n = 2 the corrected loop runs once and reads indices 0 and 1; with n = 1 it runs zero times.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Derive the legal interval from the accesses, compare the code with that interval, and only then use boundary traces to confirm the correction.

items: List every indexed expression; an omitted offset produces an incomplete constraint.
Derive their shared legal interval; the loop variable must satisfy all constraints at once.
Compare initialization and termination with that interval to locate the mismatched endpoint.
Trace the smallest legal and next-smaller inputs to verify both one-iteration and zero-iteration behavior.

items.prompt: An algorithm scans every adjacent pair in an array of length n and uses only a constant number of variables. Select its time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Each adjacent pair is inspected once.

feedback.reason: There are max(0, n - 1) adjacent pairs, and the working state does not grow with n.

blocks.text: Inspecting each pair once is linear. The fact that two array positions are read per iteration does not create a nested scan.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: There are max(0, n - 1) adjacent pairs, and the working state does not grow with n.

items: time: O(n)
auxiliary space: O(1)
O(1) time ignores that the number of adjacent pairs grows from 0 to n - 1.
O(n²) time would require a second amount of work proportional to n for each pair; reading two positions is still constant work per pair.
O(n) auxiliary space would require a separate working structure that grows with the input, but the stated algorithm uses only a constant number of variables.

items.prompt: A function scans an array once and returns an array containing every index whose value is negative. If k indices are returned, select the time, auxiliary-space, and output-space complexity.
constraints: Appending to the result is amortized O(1).
No growing collection other than the returned result is used.

feedback.reason: The scan visits n positions, while the collected indices are the required output rather than auxiliary state.

blocks.text: The function must inspect all n positions even when few or no values match, so the scan costs O(n). The loop uses constant working variables. The returned list grows with the number k of matching indices, so its O(k) size is reported separately as output space rather than auxiliary space.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: The scan visits n positions, while the collected indices are the required output rather than auxiliary state.

items: time: O(n)
auxiliary space: O(1)
output space: O(k)
O(k) time is insufficient because nonmatching positions must also be inspected; k can be 0 while n is large.
O(k) auxiliary space incorrectly counts the required returned array as temporary working state.
O(1) output space cannot hold k returned indices when k grows with the input.

items.prompt: A function must return original indices satisfying a condition. Why can sorting the array before scanning be invalid?

options.text: Sorting prevents the array from being scanned afterward.
Sorting automatically removes repeated values and shortens the array.
Sorting is invalid because it takes O(1) time.
Sorting changes which value occupies each original index unless provenance is preserved.

feedback.reason: When original positions are part of the output contract, reordering changes the meaning of an index.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Sorting changes which value occupies each original index unless provenance is preserved.”. Sorting may still be legal if each value carries its original index and the later logic restores the required provenance. Sorting alone cannot ignore that contract.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: When original positions are part of the output contract, reordering changes the meaning of an index.

items: Sorting prevents the array from being scanned afterward. — A sorted array can still be scanned; the issue is preservation of original positions.
Sorting automatically removes repeated values and shortens the array. — Sorting rearranges occurrences but does not remove them.
Sorting is invalid because it takes O(1) time. — Sorting is not generally constant time, but that is not the semantic defect here.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_never_scans: A sorted array can still be scanned; the issue is preservation of original positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_removes_duplicates: Sorting rearranges occurrences but does not remove them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_constant_time: Sorting is not generally constant time, but that is not the semantic defect here.

items.prompt: A scan must inspect every block of exactly three consecutive elements. Which loop over the block's start index is correct?

options.text: Start at 0 and continue while start < n.
Start at 0 and continue while start + 3 <= n.
Start at 0 and continue while start + 3 < n.
Start at 3 and continue while start <= n.

feedback.reason: The block occupies [start, start + 3), so its exclusive end may equal n.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Start at 0 and continue while start + 3 <= n.”. The final legal start is n - 3. This includes exactly one block when n equals 3 and no blocks when n is smaller.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The block occupies [start, start + 3), so its exclusive end may equal n.

items: Start at 0 and continue while start < n. — This permits starts whose three-element block extends past the array.
Start at 0 and continue while start + 3 < n. — This incorrectly excludes the valid final block ending exactly at n.
Start at 3 and continue while start <= n. — Starting at 3 skips the first block and misuses the block length as an initial index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_less_n: This permits starts whose three-element block extends past the array.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_plus_three_lt_n: This incorrectly excludes the valid final block ending exactly at n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_at_three: Starting at 3 skips the first block and misuses the block length as an initial index.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for deriving a safe start-index loop for accesses at start, start + 1, and start + 2.

elements.text: Identify +2 as the largest offset from start.
Rewrite the condition as start + 3 <= n.
Verify that n = 3 permits exactly start = 0.

feedback.reason: The largest indexed offset determines the upper boundary on the loop variable.

blocks.text: The accesses use offsets 0, 1, and 2, so start + 2 is the largest index touched. Keeping it at most n - 1 gives start + 2 <= n - 1, which is equivalent to start + 3 <= n. At the minimum legal length n = 3, only start = 0 passes; start = 1 would require index 3 and must fail.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The largest indexed offset determines the upper boundary on the loop variable.

items: Identify the largest offset first because it produces the tightest upper bound.
Bound the actual final access by n - 1 before rewriting the loop condition.
Convert the inclusive access bound to the equivalent exclusive-end form start + 3 <= n.
Use n = 3 to verify that the boundary admits one complete block and rejects a partial second block.

items.prompt: A candidate window has positive length w and is represented as [start, start + w) in a zero-indexed array of length n. Arrange the derivation that proves its element accesses are safe before they occur.

elements.text: Identify array[start] as the first element access.
Use the positive length w to derive array[start + w - 1] as the last element access.
Require start >= 0 and start + w - 1 <= n - 1.
Only after both bounds hold, access indices start through start + w - 1.

feedback.reason: For positive w, bounding the first and last accessed indices proves that every index between them is also inside the array.

blocks.text: The half-open window [start, start + w) includes start but excludes start + w, so its actual accesses run through start + w - 1. Requiring start >= 0 protects the lower boundary, and requiring start + w - 1 <= n - 1 protects the upper boundary. The latter is equivalent to start + w <= n; only after both hold is every intermediate access safe.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Prove safety from the first and last actual accesses; do not confuse the exclusive end start + w with an included index.

items: Identify the first included access before deriving its lower-bound requirement.
Derive the last included access from the stated positive length; the exclusive end itself is not read.
Bound both endpoint accesses; this also bounds every consecutive index between them.
Read the window only after the proof obligations hold, so an invalid candidate cannot trigger a partial access.
